analysis.one_liner: Required stock prices to be quoted in dollars and cents instead of fractions.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 31 bipartisan cosponsors and cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote, but the full Commerce Committee never acted and it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, stock prices were quoted in fractions of a dollar, with the smallest increment one-sixteenth of a dollar (about 6 cents). Dealers and exchange specialists earn money on the gap between the buy and sell price, and wide fractions keep that gap wide. This bill directed the Securities and Exchange Commission to require all stock quotes in dollars and cents, with a one-cent minimum, within a year. It never came to a vote in the full committee or on the House floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual investors. Every stock trade has a built-in cost: the spread between the price a buyer pays and the price a seller receives, which goes to the market makers in between. Fractional pricing forces that spread to be at least 6 cents per share; decimal pricing lets it shrink to a penny, so investors keep more of their own money on every trade. The bill's stated purpose is 'to protect investors and to promote efficiency, competition, and capital formation.'

how_it_helps.text: Directs the SEC to require stock quotations in dollars and cents within one year of enactment, with an implementation schedule of the SEC's choosing.

The bill's stated purpose is to protect investors and promote efficiency, competition, and capital formation; decimal pricing allows much tighter spreads than the one-sixteenth-dollar minimum tick under fractional pricing.
The proposal drew broad bipartisan support: 31 cosponsors, 14 Democrats and 17 Republicans, including both parties' leading voices on securities issues.

analysis.who_pays: Securities dealers, market makers, and exchange specialists, whose per-trade revenue depends on the spread between bid and ask prices. Decimal pricing shrinks that spread from a minimum of about 6 cents per share toward a penny, directly cutting their per-trade profit margin, and exchanges would bear the cost of converting their quoting systems.

drawbacks.text: The bill would cut the revenue dealers and exchange specialists earn from wide spreads; the industry's counterargument (not in the record here) was that wider spreads compensate them for holding risk and providing immediate liquidity, and that shrinking them might reduce that service.
Markets and brokerages would face one-time costs to convert quoting and trading systems from fractions to decimals, and the bill's one-year deadline left the SEC to set the transition schedule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad and ongoing: every investor pays the spread on every trade, so even a few cents per share adds up across millions of transactions. The costs are concentrated (lower dealer margins) and one-time (system conversion). On the merits, this was a simple, low-cost change that shifted money from intermediaries to investors.

outcome.mechanism: It got a subcommittee hearing and passed the subcommittee by voice vote, but the full House Commerce Committee never marked it up or sent it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 13, 1997 by Rep. Michael Oxley and referred to the House Committee on Commerce.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials, which held hearings on April 10 and April 16, 1997.
On May 21, 1997 the subcommittee considered and marked up the bill and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote.
The full Commerce Committee took no further action; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and it died at the end of the 105th Congress on January 3, 1999.
The bill had 31 cosponsors: 14 Democrats and 17 Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities dealers, market makers, and exchange specialists were better off: with no law requiring decimal pricing, they kept quoting stocks in fractions, preserving the wide minimum spreads they collect on each trade. Investors kept paying that built-in cost for the remainder of the Congress.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: House Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials
for.what_they_did: Held hearings in April 1997, marked the bill up, and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote.

for.name: 31 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Rep. Edward Markey (D) and Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley (R).

against.name: House Committee on Commerce leadership
against.role: Full committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Thomas Bliley, R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action after the subcommittee forwarded the bill in May 1997; the bill sat until the Congress ended.

against.name: Securities dealers and market makers
against.role: Industry that profits from the bid-ask spread
against.what_they_did: Opposed losing the wide fractional spreads; dealers argued fraction-based pricing preserved their profit on each trade, a resistance widely reported during the 1990s decimalization debate.

sides.party_line_note: Support split evenly across parties, 14 Democratic and 17 Republican cosponsors, with bipartisan original cosponsors including Rep. Markey (D) and committee Chairman Bliley (R); no member is recorded as opposing it.

industries.note: These firms earn the spread between the buy and sell price on every trade; fractional quoting with a 1/16-dollar minimum tick guarantees a spread of at least about 6 cents per share. Decimal pricing would shrink that spread toward a penny, cutting their per-trade revenue and transferring the difference back to investors.

Exchanges and their specialists share in spread revenue and would bear the cost of converting quoting systems to decimals. The bill would impose those conversion costs on them while the benefit flows to investors.
